Long before humanity dreamed of traveling beyond Earth, a mysterious red world captured our attention.
Mars.
Formed billions of years ago, this distant planet appeared in the night sky as a reddish point of light.
Ancient civilizations observed it, studied its movements, and gave it names inspired by its unusual color and appearance.
For centuries, astronomers imagined what might exist beyond its distant surface, but imagination could only take us so far.
Humanity wanted to see Mars with its own eyes, and so began one of the greatest journeys in the history of exploration.
In the early space age, humanity began sending machines towards the Red Planet.
The Soviet Union and the United States launched spacecraft into the unknown.
Many missions failed.
Some lost communication.
Others never reached their destination.
Then, in 1965, Mariner 4 successfully flew past Mars, sending back the first close-up photographs of another planet.
It was a historic moment!
Mariner 6, Mariner 7, and Mariner 9 followed, revealing more of this mysterious world.
For the first time, Mars was no longer just a distant light in our sky.
Humanity wanted more than photographs.
We wanted to reach the surface.
In 1971, Mars 2 reached the planet, but its lander crashed.
Mars 3 achieved a historic soft landing, although communication ended after only seconds.
Then came Viking 1 and Viking 2.
Their landers transmitted the first successful long-lasting surface images while their orbiters mapped the planet from above.
Later, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Mars Express, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and MAVEN expanded our understanding of Martian geology, water, atmosphere, and climate.
India's Mangalyaan, the United Arab Emirates' Hope spacecraft, and China's Tianwen-1 joined this growing exploration.
But Mars was waiting to be explored on the ground.
In 1997, Mars Pathfinder delivered Sojourner, humanity's first successful rover on another planet.
Then came Spirit and Opportunity, two robotic explorers designed for a mission of just 90 Martian days.
Spirit uncovered evidence of ancient water.
Opportunity traveled across the Martian landscape for nearly 15 years, far beyond its original mission.
Other explorers followed.
Phoenix studied Martian soil and ice.
Curiosity began investigating Gale Crater.
China's Zhurong explored the Utopia Planitia region.
And then came Perseverance, carrying advanced instruments to search for signs of ancient microbial life.
Exploration continued to evolve.
Curiosity investigated the planet's ancient environments.
Perseverance explored Jezero Crater, collecting samples for possible future return to Earth.
And above the surface, Ingenuity made history.
A small helicopter flying in the extremely thin Martian atmosphere proved that powered flight was possible on another world.
From orbiters to landers, from robotic laboratories to flying machines, every mission brought us closer to understanding Mars.
But not every explorer is still moving.
Some completed their missions and became silent witnesses on the Martian surface.
Spirit stopped communicating in 2010.
Opportunity continued for almost 15 years before a global dust storm covered its solar panels and ended its mission in 2019.
Ingenuity completed its extraordinary flight mission after rotor damage in 2024.
Other landers and spacecraft also reached the end of their operational lives.
Their journeys ended in different ways.
Some fulfilled their purpose.
Some were lost.
Some remain where their final signals disappeared.
Across the red landscape, the machines we sent to explore Mars have left behind a legacy that cannot be forgotten.
But Mars is not the end of our story.
New orbiters, advanced rovers, and sample return missions are being planned.
Missions such as Rosalind Franklin and Tianwen-3 represent the next ambitions in Martian exploration.
Scientists hope to bring pieces of Mars back to Earth.
And one day, human explorers may walk across the same landscape our machines have traveled.
Perhaps the next footprints will not belong to robots.
Perhaps they will belong to us.
Until then, the Red Planet keeps its secrets.
And the explorers we sent there remain part of our story.
Forgotten Explorers.
Their journeys may have ended.
Their stories have not.
